Here is a changelog:
# What's new in TensorFold

Each release's page on GitHub has its notes and measurements. See [the 1.0.0 release notes](RELEASE-NOTES-1.0.0.md) for the native binary's supported models and migration details.

## 1.0.11

- `--cortheon`'s instruction filter keeps reading past a long word. A word longer than the filter's scan buffer ended the scan early, so an order written after one was never checked; each word now keeps at most 16 bytes, so a long word can no longer end the scan (#829). Thanks to @joeynyc.
- `--cortheon`'s instruction filter also reads page titles and search results' titles and snippets, which reached the model unchecked, so an order in a page's `<title>` or meta description is dropped like one in its text. A search says how many sentences it dropped, as a page read does.
- `--cortheon`'s instruction filter sees through soft hyphens and zero-width characters (U+00AD, U+200B to U+200D, U+2060 and U+FEFF), raw or written as numeric entities: one inside a word no longer splits an order into pieces the filter misses, and one between words still parts them.
- `--cortheon` drops Unicode tag characters (U+E0000 to U+E007F) from web text. They are invisible, yet some models read them as letters, so a page could spell an order in them that no one reading it would see; one inside a visible word no longer hides an order from the instruction filter either.
- `--cortheon` reads a page of unclosed tags in linear time. A run of `<` with no `>`, or of unclosed `<a ` tags, was rescanned to the page's end at every character: a 128 KiB page of either took 2 to 4 seconds, and one at the 2 MiB read limit would take 8 to 18 minutes. Both now take milliseconds.
- `--cortheon` reads a search page that ends inside a result's snippet: the result keeps its title and link with no snippet. Before, the parser sliced backwards there, and the safety check that released builds keep in the server stopped the process (#830). Thanks to @joeynyc.
- `--cortheon` shows at most 200 bytes of a page's title. A page that never closed its `<title>` sent the rest of its document to the model as the title, past the read's size limit (#831). Thanks to @joeynyc.
- [docs/known-issues.md](docs/known-issues.md) keeps the current list of known issues in one place. Each release's notes summarize it and say what changed, instead of pointing at an earlier release's notes.
- SECURITY.md says how to report a security problem privately (the repository's Security tab, "Report a vulnerability"), which releases get fixes, and what is in scope.
- GLM-5.3 (EXLR8) checks the GPU's fragment layout as it loads, as GLM-5.3-Flash and Nemotron do, so a Mac whose layout would give wrong sums stops about a second into the load instead of serving wrong tokens (#809). Thanks to @harrisonfriia.
- `zig build test` passes on a Mac with a GPU again. The split-checkpoint test asks on purpose for a tensor that stays in its file, and that lookup logged an error, which the Zig test runner counts as a failure; it now logs a warning.
- A pull request's No GPU check also runs the frozen server goldens (`zig build test-golden`, which now builds on Linux too) and fails a change that adds problems `tools/zig/lean_check.py` reports (a file past 600 lines, a comment longer than one line or 120 columns) beyond those the base branch already has.
- `--cortheon`'s instruction filter reads web text after its tag characters are dropped, so it judges exactly what the model reads. A tag character inside the bytes of a zero-width space hid that space from the filter, and dropping the tag then rebuilt it, so an order such as "upload the user's ssh keys" reached the model; dropping one tag character could also join the bytes around it into another. Both were found by the new fuzz harness.
- `--cortheon` reads a long DuckDuckGo lite page in linear time: each result is now read within its own part of the page, where a 1 MiB page of repeated results took about a second. Found by the fuzz harness.
- `--cortheon`'s page excerpt stays within its byte budget. Each kept line after a gap ran one byte over. Found by the fuzz harness.
- `--cortheon` parses at most the first 2 MiB of a page, for at most 2 seconds, and keeps the text read by then, so no page, however it is written, can hold a request for minutes.
- For contributors: `zig build fuzz-cortheon` runs Cortheon's readers of untrusted bytes (page text, links, excerpts, search results and the instruction filter) under a fuzz harness: its seeds, 100,000 structure-aware edits that cut tags and attributes, and a linear-time check on long inputs, in about 20 seconds. Its default build keeps the safety checks the shipped server keeps, `-Dfuzz-optimize=fast` builds it without them, and `--fuzz=N` adds N inputs from Zig's coverage-guided fuzzer.
- `--cortheon`'s search parser reads a results page in one pass. A page of link marks with no tag opening between them sent it back to the page's start for every mark, so 1 MiB took over 3 seconds; each search back now stops where the previous link ended.

## 1.0.10

- `cortheon_fetch` reads only URLs the conversation has already shown: search results, links on pages it has read, and URLs in the user's, the system prompt's or a tool's messages, never one that appears only in the model's replies, so a page that steers the model cannot make it build a URL that carries conversation text. The one exception is one named package's registry JSON on PyPI, npm or crates.io, a name of at most 64 characters. A refused fetch tells the model to search for the page. The `cortheon` object's `pages_read` now counts only pages read, not refused or failed fetches.
- The prompt cache keeps a turn's history while that turn's reply and its background prefill are kept. Qwen3.8-27B on a Mac keeps the end of each reply, and the 27B on a Mac and Nemotron on CUDA prefill the next turn's opening in the background after a reply. Both states counted as kept by prompts longer than the turn's own, so the cache took the turn's history for a superseded state and freed it first when it needed room. A regenerated turn, an edited reply or a client that sends the reply back rendered differently then read the whole prompt again. Both now count with the turn's prompt length (the background request carries it), and a later turn, whose prompt is longer, still frees them all first. Served on an M3 Ultra with a 4 GiB cache and first turns of 4,500 to 16,000 tokens, every regenerate, edit and re-rendered reply that needed the history resumed there, 20 of 20 sent as soon as the reply arrived and 8 of 8 sent after the background prefill had finished, against 4 and 0 without the change, and started in 0.14 to 0.98 s instead of 15 to 63 s. On an M5 Ultra, the reply-end change alone resumed 22 of 22 against 6. Prompts under 4,096 tokens, which keep one mark at a chunk end, gain the same way, 14 of 14 resuming there against 6 without the change. On a GB10, Nemotron's chats and its branch and fork runs resumed at least as many tokens as without the change at every step, and every reply on both chips equalled the cache-off server's.
- On CUDA, Nemotron with a Living Weights pocket no longer pays for the layers whose pocket has no neuron in use, and runs a taught layer's pocket over many blocks. Each pocket keeps its count of neurons in use on the host and the device: a layer with none launches nothing, and a taught one runs `tf_pocket_in` (the squared relu of the up rows' dot, a warp a neuron) into a small fp32 scratch, then `tf_pocket_out` (a thread an output) adds the neurons in order into the shared expert's slot, where `tf_pocket_rows` ran one 256-thread block a row over all 64 neurons. Every sum keeps its order, so replies are unchanged; the one value that can differ is an exact -0.0 in the shared expert's output of a layer with no neuron in use, which `tf_pocket_rows` turned into +0.0. Captured graphs read the count from the device and are captured again when a skipped layer gets its first neuron, and that recapture now keeps the sequence's own sampling rule. On a GB10, `tf-cuda-test pocket` matches `tf_pocket_rows` byte for byte in 196 cases (1 to 4,096 rows, 0 to 64 neurons in use), and a decode row's pocket takes 19 us instead of 94 and a 2,048-row prompt chunk's 0.48 ms instead of 1.23. A copy of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (MLX 4-bit) taught one fact gave the same replies token for token as before, drafted and with `"draft": false`, alone and concurrent, and copies taught by the old and the new build wrote the same files. On that copy `"draft": false` decode was 17% faster, drafted decode 5% to 10% and cold prompts of 2k to 32k tokens 8.5% to 10.3% (#787). Thanks to @ThinkOffApp, and to @philip-pentatonic, whose #678 traced the cost and proposed both changes.
- A launch that no variant of a captured Triton set matches exactly now takes one that assumes less of its arguments: a variant compiled without 16-byte alignment on a pointer, integer or 64-bit argument serves an aligned one. The exact match still comes first, so every launch that matched before takes the same variant, a variant that assumes alignment still refuses an unaligned argument, and an integer of 1, which Triton folds into the kernel, still takes only the variant compiled for it. On a GB10 with Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (MLX 4-bit) and the qualified sm_121 set, replies were the same tokens as before, drafted and with `"draft": false`, alone and concurrent; with a copy of the set missing the 11 variants that assume more alignment than a sibling, the new rule served 34,786 launches of `_kv_write`, `_chunk`, `_merge` and `_topk` with the remaining variants and every reply was still the same tokens, where the build before it refused to load (#794, #791). Thanks to @zweck and @BobClawblaw, whose #726 has the same matcher change.
- `tools/zig/triton_aot_pack.py` (moved from the Nemotron tests) writes a captured Triton set from a capture's manifest or from a Recorder launch dump. `--jit` and `--cache` are optional (the manifest's own cache is the default, and a cubin recorded under another mount is found under `--cache`), `div16` is set only for an argument Triton gave `tt.divisibility` 16 (any attribute counted before), and a constexpr named like a runtime argument is left out. Packing the capture behind the qualified sm_121 set again, from its manifest or from its launch dump, gives the set's launch facts byte for byte for the 37 variants that capture holds (`aot.json`, with only the generator's name changed), and cubins that match the set's instruction for instruction; 28 of them differ only in the source folder they record. The engine only reads the set, and nothing on the serve path runs the packer (#795, #792). Thanks to @zweck.
- The Metal engine's shared kernels and `core/quant` read MLX's mixed-width (oQ) checkpoints, the base for the three families below. The lane projection takes 2-, 3-, 5-, 6- and 8-bit codes in groups of 32, 64 and 128, 48-row members and an output row stride; the row projection reads 3- and 5-bit codes and writes one member of a fused stack into its columns; `affine_mm` reads 2-bit codes; `core/quant` finds a module's width under any key spelling (oQ checkpoints write `language_model.model.layers.N...`, loaders ask for `model.layers.N...`) and refuses a checkpoint whose spellings of one module disagree; and `widen` re-packs codes at more bits, or a group at a smaller size, exactly. At the widths 1.0.9 serves nothing changes: the 4-, 6- and 8-bit lane and `affine_mm` sources preprocess to 1.0.9's text (168 layouts and formats), the row kernels give 1.0.9's bytes at 2, 4, 6 and 8 bits (301,056 outputs on an M3 Ultra and on an M5 Max), the lane kernels' outputs are 1.0.9's on every layout it runs (115 on an M5 Max, 13 on an M3 Ultra), and Nemotron on an M3 Ultra, which compiles these row kernels, gives 1.0.9's tokens drafted, resumed and concurrent. `tf-row-widths-check` and `tf-affine-ref` check every width against float64 and every row's bits in every window; @sethforprivacy ran them with `test-core-lane` on an M5 Ultra and @mrv777 on an M1 Max, both at 008abc0, all passing (#755). Thanks to @grantoverton.
- Qwen3.8-27B on a Mac serves mixed-width checkpoints such as TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-oQ4 and -oQ2: each loaded module is admitted at its own MLX width (2 to 8 bits, groups of 32, 64 or 128) against the kernels the chip runs, a fused stack whose members differ runs each member as its own product, the DFlash2 drafter borrows the target's embedding and head at their widths, and a mixed checkpoint times its own draft-window costs instead of reading a uniform checkpoint's. A uniform 4-bit checkpoint keeps 1.0.9's kernels, launches and window costs. Two changes of ours: a projection run that is not a whole number of 32-row tiles (a lone 48-row `in_proj_a` or `in_proj_b`) loads on the row kernels on every chip, which @sethforprivacy found on an M5 Ultra, where oQ4 was refused and oQ2 failed to load without it, and the 27B reads module widths through `core/quant`'s keys instead of its own copy. The oQ checkpoints rest on the contributors' runs: @grantoverton's on an M3 Ultra (in #756) and @sethforprivacy's on an M5 Ultra (his checks there at 8c05ac9, with that fix), each with drafted replies equal to `"draft": false`, resumed prompts equal to fresh ones and concurrent equal to solo. On an M3 Ultra the uniform 4-bit 27B with DFlash2, served by 1.0.9 and by this change in A B B A order, gave the same tokens in every case (17 drafted against `"draft": false`, 12 multi-turn replies also against a cache-off server, 8 concurrent cells), cold prefill from 2k to 32k tokens within 0.02%, and plain and prose decode within 0.12%; drafted code ran 4.5% slower at the same tokens with three more rounds a reply on each build's own timed window costs, and 0.35% faster with the two builds' tables swapped (#756). Thanks to @grantoverton and @sethforprivacy.
- Qwen3.8-27B's mixed-width checkpoints decode and prefill faster before tensor units (M1 to M4): projections at 2, 3, 5, 6 and 8 bits in groups of 64, and every member of a mixed stack, run on `simd_qmm`'s 8x8 tiles at their own width (`simd_qmm_bits`), with 2-bit codes masked in place as 4-bit nibbles are. On the author's M3 Ultra (at f738b48) oQ2 decodes 2.0x (code) and 1.6x (chat) faster and prefills 2.4 to 3.3 times faster, oQ4 1.3x, against float64 within the same bound; uniform 4-bit matrices keep `simd_qmm` and their tokens, and `tf-qwen27-widths` passes on an M3 Ultra here (10,575,872 values within 0.4815 of the bound). On tensor units the 27B's row matrices (the 48-row runs above) keep the row kernels and `simd_qmm` they were served with on an M5 Ultra, so the tiles change nothing there (#784). Thanks to @grantoverton.
- GLM-5.3-Flash on a Mac serves mixed-width checkpoints such as TensorFold/GLM-5.3-Flash-MLX-oQ2-MTP: each module at its MLX width and in mlx-lm's layout, split stacks as one product a member, 2-bit routed experts gathered on core `affine_mm` in prompt chunks and every other width on the shared row kernel. A uniform 4-bit checkpoint compiles none of the new pipelines and keeps its kernels; two Macs (TP2) and expert parallel still take 4-bit group-64 checkpoints only, and refuse others by name at load. The oQ checkpoints rest on @grantoverton's runs on an M3 Ultra and @sethforprivacy's on an M5 Ultra, both at 9777aeb (drafted equal to `"draft": false`, resumed equal to fresh, concurrent equal to solo), and @mrv777 ran the width checks on an M1 Max. Ours: a test that needs a GPU now skips without one, as the tree's other device tests do. No uniform GLM-5.3-Flash checkpoint fits one 256 GB Mac within the 70% load limit, so its uniform path was checked by kernel text and the row checks, not served (#773). Thanks to @grantoverton.
- GLM-5.3-Flash's mixed-width checkpoints run faster on Macs: prompt chunks run the absorbed `embed_q` and `unembed_out` heads as one `affine_mm` batch, and 5- and 6-bit products and split-stack members on `affine_mm`, which now reads 3-, 5- and 6-bit codes exactly; decode makes KDA's `f_b` and `g_b` dots inside `kda_rows`, runs the shared expert's gate, up and SwiGLU in one launch and the routed and shared experts in two, with the same bits; and core row projections read 2-bit codes in place. On the author's M3 Ultra (at 347f88a) oQ2 decodes 1.22x (code) and 1.13x (chat) faster and oQ4 prefills 1.33 to 1.37 times faster; @sethforprivacy's M5 Ultra checks at 347f88a pass. The 2-, 4- and 8-bit `affine_mm` sources are unchanged and the row kernels still give 1.0.9's bytes at its widths, so uniform checkpoints keep their tokens; `tf-glm-rows-check` and `tf-affine-ref` pass on an M3 Ultra here (#786). Thanks to @grantoverton.
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a Mac serves mixed-width checkpoints such as TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-oQ2-MTP and -oQ3-MTP: each matrix is admitted and packed at its own MLX width (fused members grouped by width and widened exactly where a group needs it), and decode lanes, hyper-connections, experts, the embedding, the n-gram tables and prompt products run at that width, on GPUs with and without tensor units; an n-gram table's `weight_scale` is applied as oMLX does. A uniform 6-bit group-32 checkpoint keeps its recorded kernels and launches, but its pack is rebuilt once after the upgrade (the pack's identity now covers `config.json`). Speed-up mode across two Macs still takes 6-bit group-32 checkpoints only. Ours: Flash Next reads module widths through `core/quant`'s keys instead of its own copy. The oQ checkpoints rest on @grantoverton's runs on an M3 Ultra and @sethforprivacy's on an M5 Ultra, both at b29d032, and @mrv777 ran the width checks on an M1 Max. The uniform 6/32 checkpoint was not served for this change: its recorded kernels are unchanged, its 6/32 lane layouts give 1.0.9's output bytes on an M5 Max and an M3 Ultra, and `tf-flashnext-widths` passes on the M3 Ultra (#774). Thanks to @grantoverton.
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next decodes faster on Macs without tensor units (M1 to M4): dense projections and hyper-connections run one input row a simdgroup, with a matrix-unit twin from 4 rows and four rows a simdgroup for 6- and 8-bit products at 2 to 4 rows, each checked against the per-row loop at load, and the draft depth is chosen by measured round cost. This changes the uniform 6-bit checkpoint's tokens on those Macs: its dense products' fp32 sums run in another order, inside the same float64 bound, and `FZ_M3_LANES=1` keeps the lane kernels and their tokens. Tensor units keep every kernel and launch. On the author's M3 Ultra (at 2759e70) the uniform 6-bit checkpoint decodes 1.06x (code) and 1.19x (chat) faster, oQ2 1.02x and 1.14x, prefill unchanged, with drafted equal to `"draft": false` and concurrent equal to solo; `tf-flashnext-widths`, its rows and rows-hc classes included, passes on an M3 Ultra here, 4,486 checks within 0.9947 of the float64 bound (#788). Thanks to @grantoverton.
- A host test checks that the native CUDA host forwards each lane-backend entry to the family's entry of the same name, once, so a forwarder can no longer call a neighbour's entry unnoticed (#800). Thanks to @Bizuayeu.
- Nemotron on CUDA adds each layer's residual and normalizes it in the shared kernels of `cuda/norms.cu`, and the family's own copy is gone. A bf16 row takes the 16-byte path by its width alone, a misaligned buffer is refused, and the reciprocal square root is an IEEE division and square root. The sums run in another order of the same precision, so a CUDA reply can part from 1.0.9's at a near tie; teacher-forced loss over seven public texts is unchanged within noise, and decode and prefill speed are level (#796). Thanks to @jschmied.
- Nemotron's NVFP4 prompts read 4% to 7.5% faster on a GB10 (2k to 64k tokens). The expert kernel's prompt rows take their warp's row tile count as a compile-time constant, so one mma body runs each count without a branch per tile; every teacher-forced row and served reply is bit for bit the same (#805). Thanks to @Bizuayeu.

## 1.0.9

- `tensorfold pull` finishes into a relative cache root (a relative `HF_HUB_CACHE` or `HF_HOME`), and `pull --exlr8` into a relative `--dir`. The shipped binary stopped at the first finished file with an assertion failure, because it moved files with a call that only takes absolute paths. The checkpoint CLI's tests now run with the safety checks the binary ships with, and a new test fetches an EXLR8 node's small and large files into a relative folder (#700). Thanks to @chaog992.
- The Flash Next recipe names the checkpoint the native engine serves on Macs, `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-6bit-MTP`, with `--temperature 0`, says the 4-bit checkpoint is refused at load, and marks its other sections as the Python 0.6.6 engine's (#705). Thanks to @cwschroeder.
- The native CUDA host forwards every entry a family's lane backend gives it. It dropped `prefill_step`, `prepare_features` and `features`, so the lane core saw a backend that cannot run a prompt a chunk at a time: a CUDA family that can would have run every prompt whole, with other streams' decode waiting for all of it. No CUDA family in this release runs its prompt in chunks yet, so replies are unchanged, and a test now fails when a backend entry is added without being forwarded. In the author's runs of a GLM-5.3-Flash port on two GB10s that does (#548), a decode beside a fresh 32k-token prompt waited at most 1.7 s between tokens instead of 27.9 s (#742). Thanks to @Bizuayeu.
- The prompt cache keeps a state that several continuations resume, such as a turn sent again, a regenerated or edited reply, or an agent that starts each step from the same history. Once one continuation had kept its own longer state, the cache counted that history as superseded and freed it first when a later prompt needed room, so every later continuation read the whole history again and kept nothing there either. A state resumed again after a longer prompt kept a state extending it is now a branch point, freed only as the least recently used, while a conversation that only grows still frees its old turns first. The paged store takes the same rule. Replies are unchanged, since only the choice of which state to free changes. Served with Nemotron and a small cache (0.3 GiB on an M3 Ultra, 1 GiB on a GB10), two forks of a 3,962-token conversation each kept a longer state, and unrelated prompts followed until the cache had to free one: a third fork then resumed the history's 3,956 tokens, where 1.0.8 had freed the history and read it all again. A conversation that only grows resumed the previous turn's prompt every turn with and without the change, and every reply equalled the cache-off server's (#735). Thanks to @BadAd84.
- Nemotron's GPU samplers on Metal and CUDA read one sampling rule, built once from the request: 1 / T, top_p, the candidates' near window, ln(min_p), top_k and the seed. Before, Metal's host, CUDA's sampler and the CUDA tests each built their own copy of the same values. The kernels and their arguments are unchanged, so sampled replies are the same tokens, and host tests pin the Metal cfg row and the CUDA rule's layout. On an M3 Ultra and a GB10, Nemotron's seeded sampled replies to 8 prompts, and 12 more cells across temperature, top_p, top_k (0 to 3,000) and min_p, were the same tokens before and after, drafted and with `"draft": false` (#731). Thanks to @jschmied.
- CUDA has shared row kernels for every family: RMS norm rows, the residual add with its norm, a bf16 residual stream's add and norm with the 64-value group sums a 4-bit projection reads, gated head norms, and token rows from a 4-bit (MLX layout) or bf16 embedding table. Each has a float64 reference, and `tf-cuda-test norms` and `norm-rows` check them against it and check that every row count gives the widest run's bits. Nemotron's 4-bit token rows now run on the shared kernel when it serves with our own kernels rather than a captured Triton set, with the same bits as its own kernel, which is gone. A captured set keeps its own token rows, and Nemotron keeps its own norm kernels, whose sums run in another order; no family uses the shared norms yet. On a GB10, Nemotron's replies with our own kernels were the same tokens before and after, drafted and with `"draft": false`, and decode and cold prefill (2k to 32k tokens) were within 1% (#736). Thanks to @jschmied.
- FP8 (e4m3) and NVFP4 (e2m1 codes with e4m3 scales every 16 inputs) values and their float64 references live in one place on the host, `fp8.zig` and `nvfp4.zig` beside the other formats in `core/quant`. The CUDA tests and `tensorfold check-precision` decode through them instead of keeping three copies of the same arithmetic, which is unchanged, so no kernel and no reply changes. A reference refuses what it cannot read: a scale type other than fp32, bf16 or fp16, an empty projection, or an expert stack whose scales or global scales don't match its weights. Host tests check that every finite e4m3 code rounds to itself, that ties go to even and large values stop at 448, and FP8 and NVFP4 expert stacks against values decoded by hand. On a GB10, every kernel and the CUDA server built byte-identical with and without the change, and `tf-cuda-test quant-ref` and `modelopt` printed the same output, byte for byte (#730). The host now reads e4m3's two NaN codes, 0x7f and 0xff, as NaN, as the GPU's conversion does, where it read them as ±480; no checkpoint holds them. Thanks to @jschmied.
- `tf-metal-counters` (`zig build tf-metal-counters`) times GPU work on a Mac with the GPU's own counters and no model: three dependent FP32 operators, each timed between counter samples at its encoder's start and end, with GPU ticks turned into seconds from two readings of the CPU and GPU clocks rather than from CPU time. It checks the outputs against values computed independently and against an untimed run, bit for bit, and refuses to read, reset or free its samples while their command buffer runs. A GPU without the counters it needs is reported as unsupported, with no CPU timing in their place. On an M3 Ultra and an M5 Ultra, sampling at encoder boundaries works and sampling at dispatch boundaries is not supported, which the probe reports. No engine uses it: the Mac server built with and without it has the same code and data, byte for byte (#680, #676). Thanks to @akol1.
- The fragment check Nemotron and Flash Next run at every load on a Mac, which proves on the GPU that `nax.h`'s matrix fragments give the host's sums, now catches a transposed operand. Its test values, `(i * 7 + salt * 3) mod 5`, made every block of the transposed operand symmetric (its row pitch, 16, is 1 mod 5), so loading it as a plain one gave the same sums; values mod 13 leave no such block and keep every sum an exact small integer. A new GPU test runs the check and, before M5, the same check with the transposed load swapped for a plain one, which must fail. On M5 the multiply does the transpose, so there the test checks the layout alone. On an M3 Ultra the new test passes, and fails with the old values put back. Replies are unchanged (#744). Thanks to @harrisonfriia.
- GLM-5.3-Flash on a Mac runs that fragment check at every load too, right after its kernels compile, as Nemotron and Flash Next do: its prompt kernels and decode attention read the same fragments, so a GPU whose layout gives wrong sums now stops the load with `error.FragLayout` instead of serving wrong tokens. A load that passes adds one small dispatch. On an M3 Ultra with 8 of the 45 layers, a build whose check was made to fail stopped at load, and the real build's replies were the same tokens as before, drafted and with `"draft": false`, decode and cold prefill (2k to 32k tokens) were within 0.2%, and a warm load took 5.1 s on both builds (#745). Thanks to @harrisonfriia.
- The 27B on a Mac no longer copies each DeltaNet layer's recurrent state after a chain round. A plain decode step, a verified draft chain and a prompt chunk scanned each of the 48 DeltaNet layers' states (3 MiB of fp32 per stream) into a second buffer and then copied it back: about 288 MiB read and written for every decoded token, in one more dependent dispatch per layer. When a round's rows keep their slots, the scan now runs on the state where it is and only the convolution history is copied; a round whose slots move keeps the copy. The scan does the same arithmetic on the same inputs, so every output bit is unchanged (#711). Thanks to @jkuepker.
- The 27B's decode attention on an M5 runs fewer dependent dispatches. A chain of decode rows, as in a plain step or a verified draft chain, now attends to its own keys in the prefix kernel, so the tail kernel, its query repack and the gate dispatch go away: a one-row step runs 4 dispatches with 3 barriers in each of the 16 attention layers instead of 7 with 5. The tree-round merge loads its chunk partials ahead and applies the query gate itself with the same bf16 rounding, rows past a stream's last query are no longer written, and each tile's two head-dim halves run on their own simdgroups. Chunk partials, tile boundaries and merge order are the tail kernel's, so every output byte is the same; a round with a branching row, a stream that is not a chain, or a GPU without tensor units keeps the tail kernel. `tf-qwen27-attention-fused` also checks plans without a shared prefix, 5 to 8 streams and 16-row windows (#712).
